msg: No 24-hour early-warning path. Art. 14(2)(a) EU 2024/2847: an actively exploited vulnerability must reach the coordinator CSIRT and ENISA within 24 hours of becoming aware. This clock is live since 11 Sep 2026.
No 72-hour notification step. Art. 14(2)(b): the vulnerability notification with corrective measures follows the early warning within 72 hours.
No 14-day final report. Art. 14(2)(c): a final report is due within 14 days of a corrective measure being available for the exploited vulnerability.
Severe incidents are on a separate clock. Art. 14(4)(c): 24-hour early warning, 72-hour incident notification, final report within 1 month. Name it separately from the vulnerability track.
No support period stated. Art. 13(8): the support period must be at least 5 years unless the product's expected lifetime is shorter, and Annex II(7) says users must be told its end date.
No coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy named. Annex I Part II(5) requires the manufacturer to put one in place and enforce it — a reporting email alone is not the policy.
No SBOM. Annex I Part II(1): vulnerabilities and components must be identified and documented, including a software bill of materials covering at the very least the top-level dependencies.
SBOM is mentioned but no machine-readable format is named. Annex I Part II(1) requires a commonly used machine-readable format — name CycloneDX or SPDX and where the file lives.

No single contact point for vulnerability reports. Annex II(2) requires a contact point where information about vulnerabilities can be reported and received — an address, a security.txt, or an advisories URL.
The reporting destination is unnamed. Art. 16 routes Art. 14 notifications through the single reporting platform ENISA operates — say that is where your 24h and 72h notifications go.

Your CRA role is undeclared. Art. 24 gives open-source software stewards a lighter regime than manufacturers, and the two owe different duties — state which one you are before someone assumes the heavier one.

No EU declaration of conformity or CE marking referenced. Art. 28 and Art. 30 make the declaration and the CE marking the visible proof of conformity for a product with digital elements placed on the EU market.

This response window is longer than the CRA clock. Once Art. 14 applies, an actively exploited vulnerability is reportable in 24 hours and notified in 72 — a 30-to-180 day disclosure window cannot be your stated obligation.

msg: Wrong CRA start date. 11 Dec 2027 is full application and Dec 2024 is entry into force; the Art. 14 reporting obligations have applied since 11 Sep 2026 and Chapter IV since 11 Jun 2026.

bad: \b(best[- ]effort|no guarantee of a (fix|response)|as[- ]is basis|we (may|might) not respond|at our sole discretion)\b
msg: This disclaimer contradicts a CRA duty. Annex I Part II(2) requires vulnerabilities to be addressed and remediated without delay throughout the support period — discretionary language does not survive it.
Stated support period is under the Art. 13(8) floor of 5 years. Shorter is only defensible when the product's expected lifetime is genuinely shorter, and that has to be said in the same breath.
The support end date you publish is already in the past. Annex II(7) makes this date the thing users rely on; a lapsed date reads as an unsupported product still on the market.
